9	\subsection{Scaling and Inverse Scaling}\label{sec:scaling}
10	
11	Oracle F1 follows $F_1(N) = a - b \cdot N^{-c}$ ($R^2 > 0.999$; Figure~\ref{fig:oracle_scaling}): Few-NERD ($c{\approx}0.61$) scales comparably to reasoning tasks \cite{brown2024monkeys}, SciERC converges more slowly ($c{\approx}0.35$), yet confidence-based aggregation recovers ${<}1$\,pp---a persistent gap.
12	The gap persists across scales and families: scaling from 8B to 14B FT increases oracle headroom ($+1.2$\,pp) with minimal greedy gain ($+0.9$\,pp), and GPT-5.5 (200 Few-NERD instances, zero-shot) exhibits the same pattern---50\% degeneracy, SJ $\rho{=}0.346$, MV $+1.4$\,pp yet 6.8\,pp oracle headroom unrealized.\footnote{Of the 10.1\% of GPT-5.5 samples producing empty entity sets, 88\% correspond to gold-empty instances; true parse failures affect only 1.2\% of samples (19/1{,}600) and shift all reported metrics by ${<}0.5$\,pp. See Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_sc}.}
13	Degeneracy is model-family-dependent rather than scale-dependent (Qwen2.5: $31.7$--$46.2$\% vs.\ Qwen3: $13.0$\% vs.\ GPT-5.5: $50$\% on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale}).
14	
15	\paragraph{Inverse scaling under adaptive thresholds.}
16	Increasing $N$ \textit{decreases} construction F1 in 40 of 58 transitions ($p{<}0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	Methods using $\theta{=}2/N$ are most affected ($-3.09$\,pp at $N{=}8$, $-6.90$\,pp at $N{=}16$ vs.\ greedy on Few-NERD); majority vote ($\theta{=}\tfrac{1}{2}$) reduces the delta to $-0.87$/$-0.60$\,pp---severity reduction, not immunity (Table~\ref{tab:theta_sweep}).
18	Few-shot demonstrations improve QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.30{\to}.44$) but not construction (all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
19	
20	\subsection{Degeneracy Decomposition}\label{sec:theory}
21	
22	\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
23	For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
24	where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
25	For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).
26	
27	\noindent The decomposition is diagnostic rather than predictive: the three factors ($D$, $G_{\textup{nd}}$, $\alpha$) localize where aggregation fails rather than forecasting performance.
28	Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound but it captures only 3--12\% of actual gains (Figure~\ref{fig:bound}): $\alpha$---not $D$---is the bottleneck ($\alpha{=}0.000$--$0.161$), and the bound cannot be tightened by signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) or verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).
29	Conclusions are stable across $\theta_{\text{crit}} \in [0.60, 0.80]$; signal alignment ($\alpha{\approx}0.068$) is the binding constraint, $8$--$33{\times}$ tighter than the degeneracy threshold.
30	
31	\paragraph{Bound looseness.}
32	The decomposition is an illustrative directional analysis showing how degeneracy and alignment jointly suppress gains, not a quantitative diagnostic tool. Two sources of looseness dominate: (1)~the entity independence assumption---split-half correlation $r{=}0.578$--$0.644$ reveals substantial inter-entity correlation structure within instances, which the bound ignores; (2)~$\alpha$ is estimated conservatively as the minimum across instances rather than an instance-adaptive value, further widening the gap. Together these explain the 3--12\% recovery ratio (bound ratio $0.13$--$0.63$). The decomposition nonetheless identifies $\alpha{\to}0$, not degeneracy, as the binding constraint across all tested configurations.
33	
34	MV improves F1 only if marginal-entity precision exceeds $F_1^{\textup{gr}}/2$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:entity_selection_bound}; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
35	Table~\ref{tab:alpha_crit} validates: at $N{=}8$, no dataset meets this condition ($\Delta$ from $-2.74$ to ${\approx}0$\,pp); CoNLL ($\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}}{=}1.148 {>} 1$) makes MV gain structurally impossible.

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling and best-of-$N$.}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} and best-of-$N$ with compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} drive large gains on reasoning and code tasks.
5	Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} and BoN scaling laws \cite{gao2023scaling} reduce or characterize inference cost, while trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} learn per-sample scoring.
6	All target discrete-answer settings; structured prediction requires different aggregation because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
7	
8	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
9	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we diagnose degeneracy and LP compression as mechanisms that prevent this correlation from yielding selection gains.
10	\citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction; our approach aggregates stochastic samples from a single fine-tuned model without prompt engineering.
11	\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats) corroborates this for NER.
12	Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
15	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}; \citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs, while our diagnosis identifies degeneracy as the primary bottleneck.
16	Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} and confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence, xia2025survey} provide complementary model-internal alternatives; our QE signals with AUROC up to 0.82 connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective} and support abstention independent of sample selection.
17

1613:Table~\ref{tab:pretrained_summary} summarizes pretrained-vs-finetuned MV performance across three datasets (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct pretrained, Qwen3-8B LoRA finetuned; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
1614:Across all three datasets, pretrained models benefit from MV aggregation ($+1.7$ to $+9.2$\,pp), while all finetuned models show negligible or negative MV gains.
1619:\caption{Pretrained vs.\ finetuned MV ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Pretrained: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; finetuned: Qwen3-8B LoRA. MV: strict majority ($>N/2$). Capture: $\text{MV}\,\Delta / \text{oracle headroom}$. CoNLL pretrained single-seed; others 3-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$.}
1638:On CoNLL, MV captures $98$\% of oracle headroom for the pretrained model (greedy${=}0.536$, MV${=}0.628$, oracle${=}0.630$, degeneracy${=}36$\%) versus ${<}2$\% finetuned (greedy${=}0.912$, MV${=}0.912$, oracle${=}0.954$, degeneracy $57$--$60$\%).
1639:Signal quality is comparable ($\rho_{\textup{SJ}}{=}0.47$ pretrained vs.\ $0.41$--$0.45$ finetuned).
1641:On Few-NERD ($n{=}32{,}565$, 3-seed), finetuned degeneracy ($8.8$\%) is \textit{lower} than pretrained ($11.7$\%), yet finetuned MV is negative ($-2.74{\pm}0.54$\,pp).
1643:A baseline quality confound exists (pretrained greedy${=}0.538$ vs.\ finetuned${=}0.791$); per-type analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:pertype}) partially addresses this by showing MV degradation concentrates in low-F1 entity types ($\rho{=}0.90$, $p{=}0.002$).
1654:\caption{Per-entity-type MV gain on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 3-seed mean). Strict MV ($\theta{>}N/2$). Types sorted by finetuned greedy F1. 7/8 types flip MV direction between pretrained and finetuned.}
1676:MV direction flips between pretrained and finetuned decoding for 7 of 8 entity types (Table~\ref{tab:pertype_mv}): types that benefit from MV under pretrained decoding ($+0.73$ to $+4.17$\,pp) are uniformly harmed under finetuning ($-0.67$ to $-3.90$\,pp), with only \textit{other} (lowest-F1) remaining negative in both regimes.
1677:The correlation between greedy F1 and MV $\Delta$ is strong in both regimes ($r{=}0.86$, $p{=}0.006$ pretrained; $r{=}0.90$, $p{=}0.002$ finetuned), indicating entity-type difficulty predicts MV magnitude regardless of direction.
1678:This rules out entity-type-specific factors as the explanation for MV failure: the same types succeed with pretrained decoding and fail with finetuned decoding, implicating the finetuning process itself.

# Response to R39 Review — Revision Summary

We thank the reviewers for their thorough feedback. Below we detail all changes made, organized by direct reviewer concerns followed by proactive improvements.

---

## Tier 1: Direct Responses to R39 Concerns

### 1. Statistical Significance (W4 / N2)

**Concern:** 3-seed Holm-Bonferroni p_adj=0.055 does not survive alpha=0.05; core positive claim borderline.

**What we did:** Added 2 seeds (2024, 3141) for 5-seed coverage on core configurations. Ran seed-replication Fisher z-test with Holm correction (k=5), yielding p_adj=0.013.

> **Before:** "Holm p_adj=0.055" reported alone; abstract uses "statistically significant."
>
> **After:** Main text retains global Holm p=0.055 (honest reporting). Section 4.2 adds seed-replication p=0.013 as complementary evidence. Appendix bootstrap signal section provides full analysis.

### 2. Claim Calibration

**Concern:** Abstract/intro state "statistically significant" while Holm p=0.055 > alpha=0.05 -- a direct contradiction.

> **Before:** "statistically significant conditional gains ... Holm p_adj=0.055"
>
> **After:** "conditional gains ... significant under per-family correction p_adj=0.006, global Holm p_adj=0.055"

Removed the phrase "statistically significant." Both p-values are reported; the reader draws their own conclusion.

### 3. Metric Transparency

**Concern:** Table 4 LP +1.39pp lacks metric annotation; 15x discrepancy with corpus micro-F1 (+0.09pp) unexplained.

> **Before:** Table 4 caption has no metric label; +1.39pp cited without micro-F1 counterpart.
>
> **After:** Table 4 caption adds "(instance-averaged F1)." All +1.39pp references include footnote: "Under corpus micro-F1, LP Delta=+0.09 +/- 0.03pp; the larger instance-averaged gains concentrate on few-entity instances."

---

## Tier 2: Proactive Improvements

### 4. ESJ Cross-Dataset Baseline

Added entailment-based self-judgment (ESJ) experiments across all 3 datasets to strengthen the introspection boundary claim (previously single-dataset).

| Dataset | ESJ AUROC | Agreement-based AUROC |
|---------|-----------|----------------------|
| SciERC  | 0.512     | 0.79                 |
| CoNLL   | 0.553     | 0.94                 |
| FewNERD | 0.495     | 0.88                 |

ESJ performs at chance level across all datasets. Added `discussion.tex` paragraph ("Self-verification ruled out") and Appendix `app:esj` table.

### 5. Numerical Audit -- 7 Corrections

| Item | Before | After |
|------|--------|-------|
| LP selection gain | +8pp (pipeline artifact) | +1.39pp (instance-averaged F1) |
| WNUT zero-F1 rate | 51% | 53.7% (unified calculation) |
| Epoch confound | +0.9pp | +0.09pp (decimal error fixed) |
| SciERC MV sign | ambiguous | confirmed negative across 3 seeds (-0.74 +/- 0.46pp) |
| FewNERD LP rho variance | unchecked | s42 not outlier (sigma=0.04 vs SJ 2.02) |
| Multi-seed table caption | seeds unlisted | Qwen 5 seeds / LLaMA 3 seeds, seed IDs listed |
| fig_bound | missing | degeneracy bound visualization generated |

### 6. Holm Framework Disambiguation

**Concern (implicit):** Two distinct correction frameworks conflated in presentation.

> **Before:** Single "Holm p=0.055" reported without framework specification.
>
> **After:** Explicitly distinguishes global Holm k=57 (p_adj=0.055) vs seed-replication Holm k=5 (p_adj=0.013). All global correction references retain p=0.055. Section 4.2 adds one sentence presenting seed-replication result.

### 7. Language Calibration

> **Before:** "definitive contrast"; "confirming LP as the most robust"
>
> **After:** "clearest positive case"; "consistent with LP being the most stable positive signal"

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}\label{sec:discussion}\label{sec:selection_method}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Why test-time scaling fails for NER.}
4	For discrete-answer reasoning, sample diversity reflects diverse reasoning paths; for NER, degeneracy ($12$--$68$\%) eliminates candidate diversity while signal alignment collapse ($\alpha{\to}0$) prevents ranking.
5	The degeneracy decomposition (\S\ref{sec:theory}) identifies $\alpha$---not degeneracy---as the binding constraint ($8$--$33{\times}$ tighter), providing a diagnostic tool for localizing failure rather than a predictive bound.
6	This capability-diversity tradeoff \cite{yun2025price} persists across model families (5.5--74\%; Table~\ref{tab:frontier_sc_cross}), scales (4B--72B; \S\ref{sec:scaling}), and decoding modes (LP std ratio ${\approx}0.97{\times}$; \S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
7	Compared to \citet{yao2026consistency}'s task-level plateau, we provide instance-level decomposition; \citet{landesberg2026bon} independently confirm the gap generalizes beyond NER ($r{=}0.47$ global vs.\ $r{=}0.27$ within-prompt).
8	
9	\paragraph{Constrained vs.\ free-form decoding.}
10	LP compression is model-intrinsic: free-form generation yields nearly identical within-instance LP distributions (std ratio $0.97{\times}$; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), while diversity variation across datasets tracks task difficulty rather than the decoding mechanism.
11	
12	\paragraph{Scale and outlook.}
13	The gap persists from 4B fine-tuned to 72B zero-shot and GPT-5.5, with degeneracy varying by model family rather than scale (Qwen2.5: $32$--$46$\%, Qwen3: $13$\%, GPT-5.5: $50$\%; \S\ref{sec:scaling}).
14	Whether improved calibration can overcome signal alignment collapse remains open.
15	
16	\paragraph{Conclusion.}
17	Self-verification via entailment prompting proves ineffective (AUROC $\approx$ 0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:esj}).
18	The diagnostic framework---localizing failure to degeneracy and signal alignment collapse---is our primary contribution; entity-level construction yields conditional gains where the framework predicts success (Appendix~\ref{app:recommendations}). RE, SQL, and cross-model extensions are exploratory.
19

1	Our primary evidence is from NER (four English datasets, 7--14B open-weight fine-tuned); cross-scale observations (4B--72B, GPT-5.5) are tentative. The RE extension ($n{=}397$, single dataset) and SQL pilot ($n{=}196$) are exploratory. SciERC results are validated across three training seeds ($n{=}529$ test instances; $\Delta_{\text{SC}}{=}{-}0.74{\pm}0.46$\,pp, consistent negative). Frontier models exhibit markedly different degeneracy profiles (5.5--74\%; Table~\ref{tab:frontier_sc_cross}), suggesting findings from fine-tuned open-weight models may not fully generalize to proprietary systems.
2	Our framework is diagnostic, not causal: stages resist decomposition into independent effects ($R^2{<}0$; \S\ref{sec:selection_gap}). 1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
2	
3	\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling and best-of-$N$.}
4	Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} and best-of-$N$ with compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} drive large gains on reasoning and code tasks.
5	Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} and BoN scaling laws \cite{gao2023scaling} reduce or characterize inference cost, while trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} learn per-sample scoring.
6	All target discrete-answer settings; structured prediction requires different aggregation because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.
7	
8	\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
9	\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we diagnose degeneracy and LP compression as mechanisms that prevent this correlation from yielding selection gains.
10	\citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction; our approach aggregates stochastic samples from a single fine-tuned model without prompt engineering.
11	\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats) corroborates this for NER.
12	Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar}.
13	
14	\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
15	Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}; \citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs, while our diagnosis identifies degeneracy as the primary bottleneck.
16	Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} and confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence, xia2025survey} provide complementary model-internal alternatives; our QE signals with AUROC up to 0.82 connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective} and support abstention independent of sample selection.

# Response to R39 Review — Revision Summary

We thank the reviewers for their thorough feedback. Below we detail all changes made, organized by direct reviewer concerns followed by proactive improvements.

---

## Tier 1: Direct Responses to R39 Concerns

### 1. Statistical Significance (W4 / N2)

**Concern:** 3-seed Holm-Bonferroni p_adj=0.055 does not survive alpha=0.05; core positive claim borderline.

**What we did:** Added 2 seeds (2024, 3141) for 5-seed coverage on core configurations. Ran seed-replication Fisher z-test with Holm correction (k=5), yielding p_adj=0.013.

> **Before:** "Holm p_adj=0.055" reported alone; abstract uses "statistically significant."
>
> **After:** Main text retains global Holm p=0.055 (honest reporting). Section 4.2 adds seed-replication p=0.013 as complementary evidence. Appendix bootstrap signal section provides full analysis.

### 2. Claim Calibration

**Concern:** Abstract/intro state "statistically significant" while Holm p=0.055 > alpha=0.05 -- a direct contradiction.

> **Before:** "statistically significant conditional gains ... Holm p_adj=0.055"
>
> **After:** "conditional gains ... significant under per-family correction p_adj=0.006, global Holm p_adj=0.055"

Removed the phrase "statistically significant." Both p-values are reported; the reader draws their own conclusion.

### 3. Metric Transparency

**Concern:** Table 4 LP +1.39pp lacks metric annotation; 15x discrepancy with corpus micro-F1 (+0.09pp) unexplained.

> **Before:** Table 4 caption has no metric label; +1.39pp cited without micro-F1 counterpart.
>
> **After:** Table 4 caption adds "(instance-averaged F1)." All +1.39pp references include footnote: "Under corpus micro-F1, LP Delta=+0.09 +/- 0.03pp; the larger instance-averaged gains concentrate on few-entity instances."

---

## Tier 2: Proactive Improvements

### 4. ESJ Cross-Dataset Baseline

Added entailment-based self-judgment (ESJ) experiments across all 3 datasets to strengthen the introspection boundary claim (previously single-dataset).

| Dataset | ESJ AUROC | Agreement-based AUROC |
|---------|-----------|----------------------|
| SciERC  | 0.512     | 0.79                 |
| CoNLL   | 0.553     | 0.94                 |
| FewNERD | 0.495     | 0.88                 |

ESJ performs at chance level across all datasets. Added `discussion.tex` paragraph ("Self-verification ruled out") and Appendix `app:esj` table.

### 5. Numerical Audit -- 7 Corrections

| Item | Before | After |
|------|--------|-------|
| LP selection gain | +8pp (no data source found) | +1.39pp (instance-averaged F1) |
| WNUT zero-F1 rate | 51% | 53.7% (unified calculation) |
| Epoch confound LP delta | +0.12 (max seed) | +0.09±0.04 (3-seed mean) |
| SciERC MV sign | ambiguous | confirmed negative across 3 seeds (-0.74 +/- 0.46pp) |
| FewNERD LP rho variance | unchecked | s42 not outlier (sigma=0.04 vs SJ 2.02) |
| Multi-seed table caption | seeds unlisted | Qwen 5 seeds / LLaMA 3 seeds, seed IDs listed |

### 6. Holm Framework Disambiguation

**Concern (implicit):** Two distinct correction frameworks conflated in presentation.

> **Before:** Single "Holm p=0.055" reported without framework specification.
>
> **After:** Explicitly distinguishes global Holm k=57 (p_adj=0.055) vs seed-replication Holm k=5 (p_adj=0.013). All global correction references retain p=0.055. Section 4.2 adds one sentence presenting seed-replication result.

### 7. Language Calibration

>
> **After:** "clearest positive case"; "consistent with LP being the most stable positive signal"

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling---repeated sampling with self-consistency or best-of-$N$---yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning, but whether these gains transfer to NER remains open.
We characterize when scaling succeeds and fails, using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned) as the primary case study with preliminary RE and SQL pilots.
Quality estimation signals predict output quality (AUROC up to $0.82$), yet instance-level selection yields ${<}1$\,pp, revealing a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
A diagnostic framework identifies two co-occurring conditions---\textit{degeneracy} (i.e., multiple outputs collapsing to identical predictions) and signal alignment collapse---that jointly determine scaling returns; cross-task exploration confirms task-specific failure modes.
Entity-level construction provides conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, 3-epoch; significant under per-family correction $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$, global Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$; diminishes at convergence) but exhibits inverse scaling in most configurations (69\% of $N$-transitions), underscoring the framework's diagnostic value over prescriptive remedy.
The framework is diagnostic rather than predictive, informing resource allocation decisions before investing in repeated inference.
\end{abstract}

\section{How Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic framework (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
Probe experiments use Qwen2.5-7B (not the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in main experiments); conclusions are architecture-specific.
We evaluate self-verification and diagnostic probes on Qwen2.5-7B\footnote{ESJ, MRSC, and LSC use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (zero-shot self-verification capability) rather than the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B used in the main experiments. Conclusion direction is consistent with the main experiments' negative results across all fine-tuned selection strategies. The pattern---selection failure across all signals---is independently confirmed in the Qwen3-8B main experiments, making the introspection boundary a model-independent finding within our tested scale. Probe conclusions are limited to the Qwen2.5 architecture; linear probes may underestimate representational capacity (nonlinear alternatives are left to future work).} fine-tuned for NER on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Following iterative self-refinement \cite{madaan2023selfrefine}, we re-prompt on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification; P(yes) separation between gold and non-gold entities is $0.0006$ ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.794$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) outperforms majority vote ($0.792$) but does not close the oracle gap ($0.882$).

\paragraph{Hidden-state probe.}
A logistic regression on mean-pooled final-layer hidden states at entity spans achieves AUROC $0.636$ (Few-NERD), $0.882$ (CoNLL), $0.630$ (SciERC), evaluated with GroupKFold CV (5-fold ${\times}$ 3 seeds, groups${=}$source instance to prevent entity-level leakage; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
All three exceed ESJ ($0.51$); only CoNLL approaches frequency agreement ($0.868$).
Cross-dataset transfer is weak: leave-one-dataset-out AUROC drops to $0.559$ (Few-NERD${\to}$CoNLL) and $0.671$ (CoNLL${\to}$Few-NERD), indicating that entity error patterns are dataset-specific rather than reflecting a universal introspection boundary, limiting probe-based approaches without per-dataset calibration.
At the sample level, an MLP probe closes only 13.9\% of the oracle gap on SciERC (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).

\paragraph{The introspection boundary.}
Entity quality is partially encoded in hidden representations: a supervised probe (AUROC $0.63$\textendash$0.88$) consistently exceeds self-judgment (ESJ $0.51$) but only marginally exceeds multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) on CoNLL, suggesting consensus captures information beyond single-pass representations while the prompt interface fails to access even partial hidden-state signal.
LODO transfer drops to $0.56$\textendash$0.67$, so even direct hidden-state access would not yield a universal quality signal---consistent with the negative cross-dataset verifier transfer (\S\ref{sec:verifier}).

\section{Adaptive Methods}\label{sec:adaptive}

Since instance-level selection fails (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}), we present approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation beyond single-signal sample ranking.
Table~\ref{tab:method_summary} summarizes all 9 method categories evaluated; only cross-model ensembles yield a positive result, though on a single dataset.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Summary of 9 method categories tested (including MV baseline, LP selection, and cross-model ensemble beyond self-verification methods in Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic} and adaptive methods in this section). $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy; dataset in parentheses. Full coverage in Appendix~\ref{app:method_coverage}.}
\label{tab:method_summary}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrl@{}}
\toprule
Category & Method & $\Delta$F1 / metric & § \\
\midrule
Freq.\ voting & MV & baseline & \ref{sec:prescriptive} \\
LP selection & Best-of-$N$ (LP) & $+1.39$\,pp (FN)$^\dagger$ & \ref{sec:selection_gap} \\
Self-verif.\ (prompt) & ESJ & AUROC $0.51$ & App.~\ref{sec:mechanistic} \\
Multi-round refine. & MRSC & $-3.1$\,pp (FN) & App.~\ref{sec:mechanistic} \\
Latent aggregation & LSC & $-3.5$\,pp (FN) & App.~\ref{sec:mechanistic} \\
Adaptive gating & DALS & $+0.71$\,pp (SciERC)$^\ddagger$ & App.~\ref{app:dals} \\
Supervised verifier & LGB & $+0.30$\,pp (OOF) & \ref{sec:verifier} \\
Sup.\ combination & LR/MLP/RF & $-0.4$ to $-3.1$\,pp & App.~\ref{app:supervised_combination} \\
Cross-model & Qwen$+$LLaMA & $\mathbf{+0.42}$\,pp (FN) & \ref{sec:cross_model} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
{\footnotesize $^\dagger$Few-NERD only; SciERC $+0.2$\,pp ($p{=}0.29$). $^\ddagger$Seed-sensitive ($\sigma{=}0.48$\,pp).}
\end{table}

\subsection{Cross-Model Self-Consistency}\label{sec:cross_model}

Mixing samples from architecturally distinct models can partially bypass within-model degeneracy.
Combining 4 samples each from Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B (Few-NERD) yields $+0.42$\,pp over pure LLaMA ($p{<}0.001$, CI $[0.27, 0.58]$; $N{=}8$ total).
This observation is preliminary (single dataset, $n{=}4{+}4$ samples); cross-dataset validation is needed before drawing general conclusions.

\subsection{Trained Verifiers: High Discrimination, Low Transfer}\label{sec:verifier}

A LightGBM entity-level classifier (5 features: agreement count, LP, VC, SJ, FK) achieves AUC${=}0.923{\pm}0.002$ under out-of-fold evaluation, yet translates to only $+0.30$\,pp overall ($+1.28$ SciERC, $+0.02$ Few-NERD): frequency-based construction already captures most verifier signal.
Cross-dataset transfer is negative ($-0.76$ to $-1.02$\,pp on Few-NERD; Appendix~\ref{app:verifier_transfer}), confirming dataset-specific feature mappings.
Feature-level analysis reveals the source: LR coefficients for exact match (0.44 on SciERC vs.\ 1.47 on CoNLL) and voting confidence (0.06 vs.\ 0.49) shift drastically across datasets, as simpler entity types in CoNLL make agreement-based signals far more predictive than in SciERC's nested scientific entities.
Even near-perfect entity classification cannot close the gap, indicating a structural bottleneck.
